topic_title: Why Do Some Startups Chase Growth Before Profit?

sources.title: Network externalities, competition, and compatibility (foundational network-effects economics)
sources.fetched_extraction: Katz and Shapiro's 1985 paper (followed by a related 1986 paper on technology adoption with network externalities, Journal of Political Economy) is the founding work of the economic theory of network effects. Core concept: a 'network externality' is a change in the benefit an individual user derives from a good as the number of OTHER users of that same good changes -- i.e., the product becomes more valuable simply because more people use it. Their related work on 'systems competition' explains why, in markets with network effects (communications networks, hardware/software platforms), popular products can become self-reinforcingly more valuable, and why the technically best product does not always win -- early leads can compound into durable advantages ('increasing returns to scale' for first movers), while early setbacks compound into disadvantages. NOTE: the original 1985/1986 papers were not directly read (paywalled); the concepts above are drawn from secondary academic summaries citing this foundational work, not the primary text itself.

sources.title: The New Rules of Growth vs. Profitability
sources.fetched_extraction: Argues growth-before-profit is rational specifically for companies with genuine network effects, which can show 'winner-take-most dynamics' and 'increasing returns to scale' -- such companies can flip from unprofitable to profitable once they reach a critical mass of users, which can make early losses a deliberate, rational bet rather than mismanagement. Cites 'Rule of 40' as an industry benchmark: top-performing software companies aim for combined revenue growth rate plus profit margin exceeding 40%; public companies tend to command the highest revenue multiples when they are high-growth AND still profitable (i.e., growth alone, without any profitability discipline, is not rewarded indefinitely). Cites customer-acquisition-cost/lifetime-value (CAC/LTV) payback period under 3-6 months as a sign of healthy underlying unit economics that can justify continued heavy investment in growth. Cites a market-structure data point: private-equity acquisitions rose from 4% of total (relevant) transactions in 2008 to 11% by 2019, which the author reads as evidence of a longer-term market shift toward rewarding profitability over pure growth. Risk / cautionary examples cited: Groupon is presented as a primary failure case, where rapid expansion masked unsustainable merchant/seller churn, and the company is argued to have lacked authentic network effects despite superficially being a marketplace. The essay also describes direct-to-consumer companies (in categories such as mattresses, shoes, and meal kits) that adopted blitzscaling-style rapid-growth tactics without an underlying network-effect or other defensibility mechanism, which the author says led to 'down rounds and investor losses' for a number of such companies. The essay also cautions that excess capital availability itself 'reduces incentives for efficiency and profits' and can obscure underlying operational weaknesses. Proposes a stage-based framework: aggressive growth (3-5x annual expansion) after product-market fit at Seed/Series A; balancing growth with efficient acquisition channels at Series B/C; gradual transition toward profitability at late stage.

sources.title: Blitzscaling: The good, the bad, and the ugly
sources.authors_or_organization: Kuratko, D.F., Holt, H.L., Neubert, E.
sources.fetched_extraction: This is a peer-reviewed business-school journal article (Business Horizons, a Kelley School of Business publication) that critically examines 'blitzscaling' -- the deliberate pursuit of extremely rapid growth, prioritizing speed over efficiency, a term popularized by LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh. NOTE: the article's full text was not accessible (paywalled) and only the citation/existence of this peer-reviewed academic treatment of the topic could be confirmed; no specific findings, data, or quotes from this paper are used as Evidence -- it is listed only to establish that 'blitzscaling' is a term with a specific, examinable academic literature behind it (both benefits and risks), corroborating the practitioner-source claims (SRC-002) from an independent scholarly venue.
